1:
What brotherly love covers is settled the same way by four, and they narrow it identically. Gill excludes love to all mankind, love to fellow-countrymen and love to natural brethren, confining it to those in the same spiritual relation and the same church state. Henry excludes the affection owed to all men as made of one blood and that owed to children of the same parents, leaving the special affection of the children of God. Ellicott corrects the English to the love of the brethren. Calvin makes the point structural, that we cannot be Christians without being brethren, the Lord having bound them by the common bond of adoption — and then turns it against his own age, the primitive custom of Christians calling one another brothers having become obsolete except among the monks, who have appropriated the word while showing by their factions whose children they are.

Why the command was needed divides them. Calvin guesses at an occasion, a secret hatred arising from the haughtiness of the Jews and threatening to rend the churches, and adds the general reason, that nothing flows away so easily as love. Henry finds two dangers: persecution, which makes the love most necessary just when it is hardest, and the disputes then running about the ceremonies of the law — disputes about religion, he says, too often produce a decay of Christian affection. Barnes reads the same verb the other way, since to bid a thing continue implies it already exists, so that these needed no reproof on the point; and Ellicott, who agrees, allows that the earlier chapters both commend their love and give ground to fear for it.

On hospitality Clarke and Calvin agree about the social fact and part over the application. There were then scarcely any public inns, so lodging a traveller was an office of charity; but Calvin observes that inns have since supplied the place, and insists the apostle commends not the hospitality of the rich but the entertaining of the needy, many at that time being fugitives from home for the name of Christ. Gill opens the door as wide as it will go, strangers meaning men of another country and unknown, wicked men not excluded; Ellicott narrows it to Christian brethren away from home, and quotes the earliest of the Fathers on the same two examples. Robertson works the grammar, where the chief idea sits in the participle, so that the sense is that some escaped notice while entertaining angels. Barnes draws out the motive: such a guest is worth more than the cost of him, and many a parent owes a child's conversion to a pious stranger in the family. Calvin meets the obvious objection, that this happens very seldom, by answering that not angels merely but Christ himself is received when the poor are received in his name. Wesley reduces it to a line, that an unknown guest may still be of more worth than he appears.

Who is meant by them that are in bonds is the sharpest division of the three verses. Gill excludes those imprisoned for crime or for debt and confines the duty to those bound for the gospel, and Clarke does the same. Barnes deliberately does the opposite, extending the word to prisoners of war, captives in dungeons, men held for trial and men held in slavery, and pressing the case of his own country's ten thousand prisoners: they are there for crime, but they are men, and they are our brothers. The closing clause divides them again three ways. Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott take being in the body of our own liability to the same suffering; Calvin reports that view and a second, that we should feel as though in their body, approves neither, and refers it to the body of the Church, so that members of one body must feel each other's evils.
4:
The first clause has no verb in the Greek, and what is supplied decides its force. Robertson states the bare fact, that the copula may be either is or let be. Gill reports both without choosing. Ellicott renders it let marriage be held in honour among all. Calvin canvasses three: an exhortation to the married to conduct themselves modestly, which he allows though he thinks the indicative would serve; a concession, that although marriage is honourable fornication remains unlawful, which he calls rigid; and his own, that the apostle sets marriage against fornication as the remedy for it, stating the way of escape before he threatens the punishment.

All five who take up the honour of marriage read the verse polemically, and they aim at different targets. Barnes is fiercest: the doctrine of the superior purity of celibacy has caused more abomination than any other opinion claiming religious sanction, and the unqualified in all proves ministers may lawfully marry. Wesley says the same in a line, clergy as well as laity, and adds that the word undefiled contradicts those who call the marriage bed licensed whoredom. Ellicott sets it against a false asceticism forbidding to marry, and supplies the occasion: laxity among the Gentiles and the prevalence of divorce among the Jews. Clarke alone finds an ancient target as well as a modern one, a Jewish sect that held marriage in little repute, and argues from nature besides, that every part of the habitable world has produced men and women in due proportion. He also reports a variant which several versions support, for rather than but, making the clause the express reason of the prohibition. Robertson defines the two classes threatened, the unmarried impure and the impure married, and observes that God judges both whether men do or not — which is Wesley's point too, that they frequently escape the sentence of men.

On covetousness Gill gives the marks of it and the reason for its mention here, that the Jews were prone to it. Clarke matches the apostle's phrase with an almost identical sentence from a Greek gnomic poet, and adds that covetousness is the vice of old age, the disposition growing with the years unless checked. Robertson notes that the compound adjective, once thought peculiar to the New Testament, now turns up in papyri and inscriptions. Ellicott borrows a judgement from a contemporary, that impurity and covetousness between them divide nearly the whole domain of human selfishness. Calvin goes underneath it to a single cause: the source of covetousness is mistrust, so that a man assured he will never be forsaken is not anxious about present things.

Where the promise comes from divides them five ways, and nobody hedges. Barnes names three passages and says the same expression stands substantially in each. Clarke traces it to what was spoken to Joshua and by David to Solomon, and holds that the apostle deliberately strengthened the wording, the Christian dispensation affording more confidence than the old covenant. Ellicott insists it occurs nowhere in exactly this form and is drawn from one text, and finds an emphasis in He Himself hath said, Scripture being treated throughout the epistle as directly spoken by God. Robertson calls it a free paraphrase of four passages, notes that a Jewish contemporary quotes it in this same form so that it may be a popular paraphrase already current, and counts five negatives reinforcing one another. Calvin declines to name any text at all, taking it for a sentence drawn from the common doctrine of Scripture. Wesley has it spoken to all believers in being spoken to three men. At the next verse Barnes turns the promise into a challenge, it remaining yet to be shown that any who simply trust God for their wants are ever forsaken, while Ellicott repunctuates the quotation from Psalm 118:6.
7:
Whether the leaders are teachers or governors is settled differently by two. Barnes says the word properly means leaders or guides, is often used of military commanders, and here denotes teachers rather than rulers, though at verse 17 it carries the other sense. Gill takes them as pastors, subordinate governors in a kingdom of which Christ is King, the Greek term being the one the Jews use for Christian bishops. Robertson calls them the founders of their church, and adds that few lessons are harder for the average Christian than good following. Calvin says men who have begotten us in Christ stand to us in the place of fathers.

Whether they died as martyrs is where the four who touch it come apart. Clarke asserts it, quoting an early Greek commentator who names Stephen and the two Jameses, and adds that such remembrance is the only worship the living owe the dead. Calvin thinks the apostle speaks especially of those who sealed their doctrine with their blood, while allowing it may be taken generally of all who persevered. Ellicott turns the silence into evidence: some had probably died a martyr's death, but the writer seems carefully to avoid saying so, his words fitting all who end their course in faith. Wesley reads a happy end and no more. Barnes agrees the noun means a going out and so an exit from the world, and uses it against the English rendering: the construction that makes the unchanging Christ the aim of those men's living is one the Greek will not bear, the next sentence standing as an absolute proposition.

That proposition also lacks a copula, and its placing is disputed. Ellicott renders it Jesus Christ is yesterday and to-day the same, yea also for ever, and makes the verse the hinge between the dead teachers and the strange doctrines. Robertson reports a commentator who would set the verb earlier, so as to yield Jesus is Christ, and prefers to place it after. What yesterday covers is disputed too: Robertson confines it to the days of Christ's flesh and the recent work of the leaders, Gill extends it past the whole Old Testament dispensation to the beginning of the world, and Clarke makes it the whole time in which there was no way to the holiest but through blood shed or typified. Then Barnes and Calvin collide outright. Barnes takes the verse for an irrefragable proof of the Saviour's divinity, since it asserts immutability, and builds perseverance on it. Calvin denies the verse is about that at all: the apostle speaks not of Christ's eternal existence but of the knowledge of him possessed by the godly in every age, and refers, as he puts it, to quality and not to essence. Henry stands with Barnes, the Bishop of their souls being ever the same, as merciful and powerful in the Old Testament day as in the gospel day.

At the warning against strange doctrines the manuscripts divide the verb. Clarke reports that almost every important copy and version reads not carried about but carried away, calls it undoubtedly true, and glosses it do not apostatize; Ellicott agrees and suggests the common reading drifted in from Ephesians 4:14. On what the doctrines were, Ellicott argues from the contrast inside the verse — its subject is meats and not grace, and its promoters serve the tabernacle. Clarke identifies the meats as the Levitical sacrifices, so called because the offerers feasted on them once the blood had been poured out. Robertson enters the caveat nobody else enters, that the new is not always wrong any more than the old is always right. Calvin reduces the whole to one point, that every error arises from not abiding in Christ alone, and turns it against the Roman remedy for error, which he says is to bury the knowledge of Christ.
10:
What the altar is divides them, and Gill states the alternatives before rejecting two of them. It is not the cross on which Christ was crucified, nor the Lord's table where his flesh and blood are presented to faith, but Christ himself, who is altar, sacrifice and priest together; and Gill reads the furniture of the old altar as figure throughout, the shittim wood and brass for incorruptibility and strength, the horns at the corners for the refuge of those who flee from the four corners of the earth. Barnes takes the altar to be evidently the cross, Clarke puts the altar for the sacrifice on it, and Wesley says flatly that it is the cross of Christ. Robertson keeps it abstract, a spiritual altar and not a literal one, the metaphor being carried through the passage.

Who is excluded from eating is agreed, and why is not. Barnes explains from the law of maintenance: a part of the meat offered in sacrifice became the property of the priests and Levites by right, and the apostle's point is that there is a higher sacrifice they have no right to while they remain in the service of the tabernacle, that is, while they remain Jews. Calvin grounds it instead on the particular rite of the day of atonement, where no part of the victim returned to the priests at all — so that the exclusion is not a penalty but the fulfilment of the type, and to partake of Christ we must renounce the tabernacle, the word standing for the whole apparatus of ceremonies. Robertson takes the same word for the whole ceremonial economy of Judaism, and Wesley for adherence to the Mosaic law.

The burning outside the camp is then read two ways. Clarke reports an opinion that the entire consumption of the sin-offering was meant to show that sin was not pardoned by such offerings: since eating the other sacrifices intimated a share in the benefits procured, being forbidden to eat the sin-offering proved they had no benefit from it and must look elsewhere — so that those who continued to offer and refused the Christ had no right to the blessings procured by him and could get none from their own. Gill identifies the beasts precisely, not the red heifer nor the sin offering generally but the bullock and goat of the day of atonement, and matches each step of the rite to a step in the passion. Barnes corrects the connecting particle, which he says should be rendered moreover rather than for, since a fresh consideration is being introduced and not a reason for what precedes; he adds that the custom outlived the wilderness, the body being carried beyond the walls of Jerusalem after the temple was built, on the principle that what was unlawful in the camp remained unlawful in the city. Robertson notes that this is the only place in either Testament where the general word for animal is used of a sacrificial victim.

On the suffering outside the gate, Barnes alone asks how it came about, and answers that it was secured by Jesus being put to death after a judicial process rather than in a popular tumult, since no criminal was executed within the walls; he adds that the place shown as Calvary now stands inside the walls and cannot be the site. Clarke reads the departure as symbolic of more than the sacrifice: Christ left the city, denounced its destruction and abandoned it to its fate, and suffered outside to bring the Gentiles in. Ellicott keeps to the correspondence, the gate and the camp each denoting what lay beyond the dwelling-place of God's people, so that Christ fulfilled the law of atonement in this point as in every other. Wesley says the gate of Jerusalem answered to the old camp of Israel.
13:
What camp we are to leave is answered at two different levels. Wesley, Clarke and Robertson make it the Jewish dispensation, Robertson putting it as a choice — if a separation must come between Judaism and Christianity then Judaism is what we give up — and calling this the great passionate plea of the whole epistle. Ellicott turns it into an individual demand: each must choose for himself between the synagogue and the church, since between the two there can be no fellowship. Gill allows that sense and adds the camp of this world, so called for its instability, hostility, noise and multitude, so that going forth means having the affections weaned rather than changing a religion. Calvin puts the cost in front: the way out runs through exiles, flights and reproaches, a warfare in which we must strive even to blood, set against the shadowy practices the teachers of ceremonies boasted of. Barnes makes it a test of the reader — many profess to love Christ while religion costs them no reproach who would have shrunk from following him to Calvary.

The next verse draws an argument about the date of the letter. Clarke reads it as an allusion to the approaching destruction of Jerusalem and reckons the interval at seven or eight years. Robertson reports the inference drawn from the same words, that the epistle must predate that destruction, since afterwards a reference to it could hardly have been avoided. Ellicott makes the same observation without the inference, remarking how impressive the words become in the light of events then unlooked for and so near. Barnes reads the verse pastorally instead, as comfort for readers who were about to be driven from the city into exile. Calvin generalises furthest: those who enjoy a quiet life imagine they have a rest in this world, and it is therefore profitable to be often tossed about, that men inclined to look downwards may learn to look up.

At the sacrifice of praise Clarke produces a rabbinic maxim, that in the time of the Messiah all sacrifice shall cease except the sacrifice of praise, which turns the Jewish authorities themselves into witnesses that the system is over. Barnes explains the phrase from the peace-offering, which was designed not to produce peace with God but to preserve it, the offerer standing already in the relation of a friend. Ellicott identifies it with the thank-offering of the law. The quotation behind the fruit of the lips then divides three of them. Clarke notes that the Greek version reads fruit where the Hebrew has the heifers of our lips. Ellicott says the Hebrew differs in expression but not in meaning, rendering the lips as bullocks, that is, as sacrifices. Calvin goes further into the grammar, holding the Hebrew words to stand in apposition and not in construction, so that the sense is we will render calves, our lips, the Targum reading it his way and the Vulgate the other.

On the second sacrifice they converge and then differ over its weight. Robertson notes that the three great definitions of worship in the New Testament are all inward and ethical. Calvin makes every act of love a sacrifice, and adds that the elements of the law are now not merely superfluous but harmful, as drawing men away from the right way of sacrificing. Clarke presses it hardest: no reliance even on the infinitely meritorious sacrifice of Christ is acceptable in a man who has no charity towards his neighbour, and one who does not bear this fruit shows, whatever his creed, that he is no Christian. Barnes grounds the pleasure God takes in it on God's own nature, since he does good continually. Gill extends the beneficence to enemies as well as friends, and Henry limits it by ability, according to our power, to the necessities of the souls and bodies of men.
17:
Chrysostom argues the command from the alternative rather than the text, by a run of images: remove the leader from a chorus and it loses time and order, the commander from a phalanx and the evolutions fail, the helmsman from a ship and you sink her, the shepherd from a flock and all is destroyed. He then ranks the evils. Anarchy is an evil; disobedience is no less an evil, since a people that will not obey is like a people with none, and worse, having no excuse; but a bad ruler is worse than either, and it is better to be led by nobody than by a wicked man.

Four others limit the obedience, each in a different place. Barnes divides what may be commanded into three sorts — what God has positively enjoined, always to be obeyed; what a society has agreed on as needful, binding unless it violates conscience; and matters of convenience, where the rulers should judge — and rules that the obligation never reaches what is wrong in itself. Wesley draws the line inside the person: give up not your conscience or your judgment but your own will, and only in things purely indifferent. Calvin puts the limit on the ruler: the apostle speaks only of those who faithfully perform the office, and men who have nothing but the title, or use it to destroy the Church, deserve little reverence and less confidence. Gill and Barnes agree on who is not meant: not the Jewish authorities, whose tutelage was over, and not civil magistrates, there being as yet no Christian magistrates at all.

On the second verb they collect renderings. Calvin reports four — to concede, to be compliant, to submit with becoming respect, to obey promptly — and takes the point to be a submissive mind rather than an outward act. Ellicott renders it yield, so that besides fulfilling injunctions one complies with wishes. Robertson notes the compound means to yield under and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, as does the closing adjective, which he glosses not merely unprofitable but hurtful. On the watching Ellicott makes the Greek emphatic, it is they that watch on behalf of your souls, and warns that watching with grief both weakens their hands and brings displeasure on the flock. Clarke adds that many pastors who loved their flocks as their own souls will be obliged to accuse them before God. Wesley makes it a test of the pastor: he is no good shepherd who neither rejoices over them nor groans for them, and if the groans of other creatures are heard, how much more these.

At the request for prayer the interesting question is what the writer claims for himself, and a variant decides it. Henry builds on the modesty of the received text: many of the Jews thought ill of the apostle for having cast off the Levitical law, and he might have said we know we have a good conscience but chose to say we trust, which teaches us not to be too confident of ourselves. Ellicott reports that a change in the Greek requires instead we are persuaded that we have a good conscience, which removes the modesty Henry rests his lesson on, and infers from the request itself that some mistrust of the writer's motives must have existed in that church. He also observes that the plural is not used of himself alone, since the next verse shifts to the singular, though whether he joins himself to the rulers or to his fellow labourers cannot be told. Barnes states the condition of any such request: only a man who aims at right and keeps a good conscience can properly ask the prayers of others. Gill grounds it on the arduousness of the work, and Clarke on the Church's weakness, which he says is dark and poor because it prays little.
20:
Why God is addressed as the God of peace is answered from the word, then from the situation. Clarke says peace among the Hebrews means prosperity of every kind, so the title is the God of all blessedness; Barnes takes it for every happiness, opposed to whatever disturbs the mind; Gill observes that one version makes the God of peace to be Christ himself, though the next clause distinguishes them. Ellicott argues from usage to occasion: in almost every parallel place the context suggests strife to be brought to rest, so the title is chosen for the divisions just hinted at and the unrest the epistle exists to remove.

Where the clause about the blood attaches is the crux, and Barnes refuses the English outright: the phrase is not joined to the raising, and he asks what sense there could be in raising Christ from the dead by the blood of the covenant. In the Greek, he says, the shepherd is great by that blood, and so was constituted the great Ruler of his people. Ellicott and Robertson attach it to the bringing up rather than the greatness, Robertson taking the language from Zechariah 9:11 and noting how it recalls Christ's own words about the blood of the covenant. Calvin renders the preposition in rather than by, and draws a doctrine from it: Christ so rose that his death retains its efficacy for ever.

Which prophecy stands behind the shepherd divides them again. Clarke gathers three passages in which the title is given to Christ, and treats the phrase as their common property. Ellicott and Robertson pin it to one, Isaiah 63:11, where the Greek version asks who raised up out of the sea the shepherd of the sheep — Moses brought up from the sea to shepherd Israel, and by the same hand the great Shepherd brought up from the dead — Robertson adding that the epithet great is the writer's own, and that this is the only direct mention of the resurrection in the letter. Clarke supplies the reason the raising is ascribed to the Father, that God's acceptance of the sacrifice is signified by his raising Christ's human nature. Cyril leaves the syntax aside and reads the descent through the prophet swallowed by the fish, who cried out of the belly of hell though he was in the whale, and whose head went down to the chasms of the mountains, taken for the sepulchre hewn out of rock.

The prayer that follows turns on one verb, and the two who define it end in opposite places. Barnes glosses it to make fully ready, to put in full order, and adds that the apostle does not affirm they were then perfect or would be in this life; the prayer is for grace sufficient to do God's will. Clarke glosses it to put completely in joint, and takes it as far as it will go: a complete change in the whole soul, cleansed from all sin because God can be pleased with nothing unholy, then an outward conformity answering to it, both produced by the blood. Ellicott separates two words the epistle renders alike, one opposed to what is immature and the other meaning completeness of equipment, and notes that the best authorities read every good thing rather than every good work. Calvin draws from the word a doctrine of dependence: we are not fit to do good until God forms us for it, nor shall we continue unless he strengthens us, perseverance being his peculiar gift; and what is asked is not the first impression but the polishing. Gill measures a good work by the revealed will of God, so whatever lacks that warrant is none, however religious its appearance. Wesley reads the covenant as the Christian one, not temporary like the Jewish, and turns the petition into a wish for holiness inward and outward.
22:
Why the writer should have to beg a hearing at all is answered from his standing by two and from human nature by two others. Gill notes he speaks by entreaty rather than authority, being the apostle of the Gentiles and no favourite with the Jews for having preached down the ceremonies of the law. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the argument just concluded: having shown the Levitical system insufficient, declared it abolished, and announced that their city was shortly to be destroyed, he might well suppose his readers prejudiced against him. Henry generalises past the occasion, that men are so bad, believers included, that even the most comfortable doctrine delivered with the most convincing evidence needs an earnest entreaty that they will bear it and not fall out with it. Robertson simply takes the phrase for the writer's own description of the whole letter.

In what sense the letter is brief divides them further. Barnes denies the obvious reading outright: it is not short compared with the writer's other epistles, most of which are shorter, but brief compared with the weight and difficulty of the subjects, which could have borne a far longer treatment — and he observes that the thoughts of this epistle are easily expanded into volumes, and that it can hardly be explained without a commentary far exceeding the text. Wesley says almost the same in a line, longer than his usual letters yet few words considering the copiousness of the subject. Ellicott measures it by the clock instead, a letter that could be read to the assembled church in less than an hour. Robertson notes that the idiom occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and Clarke prefers to render it simply that he has written briefly. Calvin refuses the whole line of explanation. The brevity is mentioned, he thinks, so that the writer may not seem to be diminishing the ordinary work of teaching: Scripture was not given to silence the voice of pastors, and men should not be fastidious when the same exhortations sound often in their ears — the more so because, being naturally anxious to learn, they would rather hear something new than be reminded of what they know, and being slothful can ill bear to be stimulated and reproved.

The notice about Timothy raises two questions, and the second is the larger. On the first, whether he had been released from prison or despatched on an errand, Gill takes the release, and supposes him to have been a prisoner for the gospel and perhaps a fellow prisoner at Rome. Barnes argues from the connexion for the other sense, since the writer speaks of him as away and hopes he may soon return. Clarke presses the same case on external grounds: there is no evidence Timothy was ever imprisoned, and in none of the letters written during the Roman confinement, through most of which Timothy was present, is there any hint of it; he suggests instead the mission into Macedonia. Clarke also reports that the possessive in our brother, supplied by the translators, is very probably genuine, being found in several uncials and versions.

The second question is who wrote the letter, and the same clause is made to answer it two ways. Barnes takes the affectionate mention of Timothy as a brother for a strong circumstance showing the author was Paul, since no other apostle would naturally have used the term of him. Clarke draws a different inference from the following words, that whoever wrote it was at liberty when he wrote, having the disposal of his own time — and he leaves the identification open, saying Paul himself, or the writer of this epistle. Ellicott, who elsewhere in the chapter speaks of the writer as a disciple of Paul rather than Paul, offers no support to the traditional ascription here.
24:
Calvin asks the question the others pass over: in a letter written to the Hebrews generally, why should some be greeted apart from the rest? His answer is that the salutation goes particularly to the rulers as a mark of honour, so that the writer might conciliate them and lead them gently to assent to his doctrine — a piece of tactics rather than courtesy. On the saints added to them he offers two possibilities, that the Gentile believers are meant, so that both parties might learn to cultivate unity, or that those who first received the letter were being told to pass it on. Gill reads the repeated all as a deliberate universality, high and low, rich and poor, stronger and weaker believers alike. Clarke uses the word to make a historical observation, that a Christian was then a saint by profession and most were so in fact, whereas in process of time the title came to be applied to everyone bearing the Christian name — as the same honourable words were applied to the Jewish nation when its piety and morality were at a very low ebb. He adds that greetings between churches that had never seen each other show how deep the brotherly feeling ran.

The greeting from Italy is then made to do quite different work. Barnes takes it as evidence of provenance and says the writer was in Italy and probably at Rome; Clarke reads it the same way and adds that he had not yet moved after his release, and that those greeting were probably the Jews there who had embraced the faith. Ellicott refuses to decide, since the words are consistent with two hypotheses — that the writer is in Italy and salutes his readers in the name of Italian Christians, or that he is writing to a church in Italy and sending greetings from Italians who are now with him. Robertson states the same alternative in a sentence. Barnes also notices an anomaly he cannot explain, that nobody is named here, as is usual in the epistles of Paul, and says the cause of the omission is unknown.

At the closing benediction three of them turn from the text to the note appended after it, and all three deny it any weight. Barnes calls the subscription of no authority and goes further, calling it demonstrably erroneous, since it makes Timothy the bearer while the letter itself says he was absent. Clarke sets the versions and manuscripts side by side to show how little they agree: one has the letter written from Roman Italy and sent by Timothy, another has only that the epistle is completed, another that it was written in Italy and sent by Timothy, one great uncial that it was written from Rome, and the printed editions differ again. Ellicott supplies the decisive point, that no manuscript earlier than the ninth century carries the subscription in its familiar form, and that no ancient copy has more than the bare words to the Hebrews, except the one which adds that it was written from Rome. From this he draws the conclusion that matters: the mention of Rome or Italy is itself drawn from the salutation in the previous verse, and the reference to Timothy may rest on nothing but the notice before that — so the tradition is not independent testimony but an inference from the text, and an old interpretation took even that notice of Timothy to mean a departure on some mission rather than a release from captivity. Gill, who does not enter the question, reads the benediction as the writer's usual close and expands it into renewed discoveries of God's favour, fresh communications of grace, and an increase of grace within and gifts without; Ellicott notes the same brief form stands at the end of four other letters.
